law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.q: Why does the prompt explicitly forbid the AI from characterizing a clause as "enforceable," "standard," or "favorable"?
options: That is a legal judgment only the attorney can make, and the tool should describe the text, not practice law
Those words are too complex for the AI to use accurately
It makes the summary too long
Clients dislike seeing evaluative language in summaries
law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.why: Banning characterizations like enforceability or favorability keeps the tool in the lane of describing the text, leaving legal judgment entirely to the attorney.

law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.q: The AI's summary states "Not stated" for a renewal notice period. What should the attorney do with that flag?
options: Accept it at face value without checking, since the AI already reviewed the text
Go back and confirm the document genuinely doesn't address that point before relying on the flag
Delete that section from the summary since it adds no value
Ask the AI to guess a typical renewal notice period instead
law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.why: Accepting a 'Not stated' answer without going back to confirm the document genuinely doesn't address that point is a listed common mistake; the flag should prompt verification, not blind trust.

law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.q: A paralegal wants to paste an unredacted client contract into a personal-tier consumer AI account that isn't approved by the firm for confidential data. What's the concern?
options: It's only a minor style issue since the summary will be reviewed anyway
There's no concern as long as the summary itself doesn't mention the client's name
It's a confidentiality and ethics risk, not just a style issue, and requires firm approval or redaction first
It's fine because the AI provider promises not to retain data
law-b1-summarize-legal-documents-with-gr.why: Pasting an unredacted document with client-identifying details into a non-approved consumer AI account is explicitly flagged as a confidentiality and ethics risk, not merely a stylistic concern.

law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.q: Why does the extraction prompt require a source clause citation for every row of the table?
options: It's required by court formatting rules
It makes the table print correctly
It allows the AI to skip verifying dates
It turns the extraction into something auditable in seconds, rather than requiring a full re-read of the document
law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.why: Requiring a source clause for every row lets the extraction be audited quickly against the original document instead of needing a full re-read.

law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.q: An extracted deadline needs to go into the firm's docketing calendar. What must happen first?
options: It must be checked against the original clause before being entered into the calendar
It can be entered directly since the AI was instructed not to infer dates
It should be rounded to the nearest business day automatically
A second AI tool should independently generate the same deadline for confirmation
law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.why: Letting an extracted deadline go straight into a calendar or docket without checking it against the original clause first is a listed common mistake, given how consequential a missed or wrong deadline is.

law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.q: The document doesn't specify a governing law clause. What should appear in that field of the extraction table?
options: The AI's best guess based on where the parties are likely located
"Not stated," since the rule requires flagging unstated facts rather than assuming a typical value
The governing law from a similar contract type
The field should be left blank with no explanation
law-b2-extract-parties-dates-and-obligat.why: The prompt requires writing 'Not stated' when a fact isn't in the document, rather than estimating or assuming a typical value like a default governing law.

law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.q: Why does this lesson feed the AI your own already-verified notes rather than the raw source documents directly?
options: Raw documents are too large for the AI to process
It saves money on AI usage costs
A summary-of-a-summary compounds risk if the model is also asked to interpret primary material at the same time
Raw documents must always be reviewed by a paralegal first
law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.why: Using your own verified notes instead of raw documents avoids compounding risk, since the model would otherwise be interpreting primary material and organizing it in the same pass.

law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.q: Your notes don't mention any next steps for the matter. What should the memo's "Next Steps" section say?
options: The AI should infer likely next steps based on similar matters
The section should be deleted from the memo entirely
The AI should ask the attorney a follow-up question before finishing
"Not specified in notes," rather than the AI inventing plausible next steps
law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.why: The prompt requires writing 'Not specified in notes' when the source notes don't state next steps, preventing the memo from looking more complete than the attorney's actual knowledge.

law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.q: Before circulating an AI-assisted internal matter summary to colleagues, what label should it carry?
options: "Internal use - AI-assisted draft, attorney reviewed"
No label is needed since it was generated from verified notes
"Confidential - do not distribute" only
"Final - approved for court filing"
law-b3-internal-matter-summaries.why: Circulating the memo without an 'AI-assisted draft, attorney reviewed' label risks a colleague treating it as an authoritative final record rather than a reviewed working document.

law-b4-draft-client-communications.q: In the draft client status update, a sentence would require the attorney's legal judgment about the strength of the matter. What should the AI do at that point?
options: Write the most likely conclusion based on the facts given
Insert a bracketed placeholder like [ATTORNEY TO ADD ADVICE HERE] rather than writing something plausible-sounding
Omit that part of the update silently
Add a general disclaimer instead of addressing the point
law-b4-draft-client-communications.why: The bracketed-placeholder instruction is the key safeguard: it visibly marks exactly where the attorney's judgment must go instead of letting the model guess at advice-adjacent language.

law-b4-draft-client-communications.q: An associate reviews an AI-drafted client email, decides it looks fine, and sends it directly from the AI tool's export feature. What went wrong?
options: Nothing, since the draft was labeled "DRAFT - NOT FOR SENDING"
The associate should have used a different AI tool for sending
An AI-generated client email should never be sent without the attorney personally reviewing, editing, and sending it themselves
The email should have been shorter before sending
law-b4-draft-client-communications.why: The workflow requires the attorney to personally review, edit, and send the communication themselves; sending an AI draft unedited is a listed common mistake.

law-b4-draft-client-communications.q: Why does the prompt instruct the AI not to explain a delay or predict next steps unless the attorney actually supplied that information?
options: Because clients don't want to know about delays
Because it would make the email too long
Because delays are always confidential
Because inventing a reason for delay or a next step not actually given creates a risk of misleading the client
law-b4-draft-client-communications.why: Asking the model to explain a delay or predict next steps without being given that information is a listed common mistake, since it risks the draft stating something the attorney never actually determined.

law-i1-document-review-checklists.q: Why does the prompt require checklist items to be phrased as questions ("Does the assignment clause require consent?") rather than assertions ("The assignment clause must require consent")?
options: Phrasing as questions keeps the tool from quietly injecting legal conclusions into what should be a neutral review aid
Questions are shorter to read
Assertions are not supported by most AI models
It's required by bar association formatting rules
law-i1-document-review-checklists.why: Framing checklist items as questions rather than conclusions prevents the AI from injecting legal conclusions into what is meant to be a neutral review aid, not authoritative guidance.

law-i1-document-review-checklists.q: A checklist item is tagged [VERIFY CURRENT LAW]. What does this tag signal to the reviewing attorney?
options: That item can be safely skipped since the AI already checked it
That the checklist's usefulness ends there and the attorney's own current-law research must begin
That the clause is definitely non-compliant
That the item only applies to federal jurisdictions
law-i1-document-review-checklists.why: The [VERIFY CURRENT LAW] tag flags exactly where the checklist stops being useful on its own, since the model cannot confirm what current statutes or local rules actually require.

law-i1-document-review-checklists.q: A firm already has an existing playbook checklist for lease reviews. What should happen when generating a new AI-assisted checklist?
options: The existing playbook should be discarded in favor of the AI's generic version
Both versions should be used interchangeably at random
The AI should build on and refine the existing playbook rather than replace it with generic content
The playbook should only be referenced for very short leases
law-i1-document-review-checklists.why: Letting the checklist replace the firm's actual playbook instead of building on and refining it is a listed common mistake; the AI output should extend real firm standards, not override them.

law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.q: Why is the AI-generated clause-by-clause comparison described as a "screening tool" rather than the authoritative record of what changed?
options: Because it only works on short documents
Because it cannot compare more than two clauses at a time
Because it requires a paid subscription to be accurate
Because word-processor track-changes or a manual line-by-line pass remains the authoritative check before anything gets signed off
law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.why: The AI comparison is useful for surfacing likely areas of change quickly, but track-changes or a manual pass remains the authoritative check before signing off on anything.

law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.q: The AI flags a possible change as "Uncertain - verify manually." What is the appropriate response?
options: Treat it as a signal to check that section manually rather than asserting a difference confidently either way
Ignore the flag since uncertain items are rarely real changes
Automatically treat it as a substantive change
Ask the AI to just guess with higher confidence
law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.why: The 'Uncertain - verify manually' fallback exists because text comparison over long pasted documents can misalign paragraphs or miss changes, and this exact type of error must never reach a signature page unverified.

law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.q: Why does the prompt ban the AI from stating which version is more favorable to either party?
options: It would make the output too long
Favorability assessment is a negotiation judgment call for the attorney, not something the model should assert
Favorability can never be determined from contract text
It violates the AI tool's usage policy
law-i2-compare-two-document-versions.why: The prompt instructs the model to describe changes only, not state favorability, because that is a judgment call for the attorney informed by the broader negotiation context.

law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.q: Why must the model generate open, neutral questions rather than leading ones when prepping for a witness interview?
options: Leading questions take longer for the AI to generate
Neutral questions are always shorter
Leading questions can affect the value of the answer in an interview or witness context
It has no real effect on interview quality
law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.why: Letting a leading question slip through unedited into a witness interview is a listed common mistake because leading phrasing can affect the value of the answer received.

law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.q: A paralegal wants to paste deposition excerpts into a personal, non-firm-approved AI tool to generate interview questions faster. What's the concern?
options: No concern, since interview prep isn't legal advice
The concern only applies to signed contracts, not deposition material
It's fine as long as client names are removed from the file name
Deposition excerpts and case notes are often privileged or work product, and pasting them into a non-approved tool can raise real confidentiality and privilege concerns
law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.why: Case material like deposition excerpts is often privileged or attorney work product, and pasting it into a non-approved consumer AI tool risks a waiver issue, not just a style problem.

law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.q: The AI generates 15 questions grouped by purpose for an upcoming client meeting. What should the attorney do before the meeting?
options: Select and prioritize the questions themselves, since the AI list is a starting menu, not a final agenda
Use the list verbatim as the meeting agenda, in the order generated
Send the full list to the client in advance for approval
Discard the list and start over, since AI-generated questions can't be trusted
law-i3-meeting-prep-questions-from-case-.why: Using the generated list as the meeting agenda verbatim instead of selecting and reordering based on what matters is a listed common mistake; the attorney must prioritize using their own judgment.

law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.q: Claude answers a research question inside a matter's Project and cites a specific uploaded case excerpt. What does this citation actually guarantee?
options: That the cited case is correctly quoted and still good law
Only that the answer is drawn from what was uploaded, not that the underlying citation is accurate or current
That the case has been Shepardized automatically
That the case is binding in the relevant jurisdiction
law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.why: Grounding in uploaded sources only guarantees Claude drew from what was given to it, not that the citation is accurate, current, or the right version of a statute — that must be verified independently.

law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.q: Why is it important to independently verify every case citation against the actual reporter or statute before it appears in a filing?
options: Because Claude is slower than other tools
Because it is only a formatting requirement
Because courts have sanctioned attorneys for filing briefs with AI-generated citations that were fabricated or misstated
Because uploaded PDFs sometimes fail to render
law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.why: Courts have sanctioned lawyers for filing briefs with fabricated or misstated AI-generated citations, which is why independent verification against the primary source is described as not optional.

law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.q: What is the recommended way to use a Claude Project for legal research, according to the pro tip?
options: Upload broad, unverified sources to discover new authority you haven't checked yet
Avoid labeling sources so answers stay general
Use it as a replacement for pulling the actual case reporter
Upload only case excerpts and statute sections you've already pulled and confirmed are current, and use it to organize verified research
law-i4-organize-research-notes-with-note.why: The pro tip recommends uploading only already-verified, current sources and using the Claude Project to organize that research, not to discover new, unchecked authority.

law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.q: Why does the framework separate fixed guardrails (grounding rules, non-final labeling, no-advice language) from variable placeholders (document type, jurisdiction)?
options: It ensures the safety language never gets accidentally dropped because someone filling in the brackets was in a hurry
It makes the template shorter overall
Placeholders and guardrails cannot technically coexist in one prompt
It's required for the template to be searchable
law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.why: Separating fixed guardrails from variable placeholders means anyone on the team fills in the brackets while the safety language stays intact regardless of how quickly they're working.

law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.q: A firm builds a framework so broad it says "analyze any legal document." What problem does this create?
options: It becomes too fast to be useful
The variable parts swamp the fixed guardrails and output quality becomes inconsistent again, defeating the purpose of standardization
It requires more storage space
It can no longer be versioned
law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.why: Building a framework too broad is a listed common mistake: it lets the variable parts overwhelm the fixed guardrails, reintroducing the inconsistent quality the framework was meant to solve.

law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.q: Why does the lesson recommend testing the framework on 2-3 real or realistic documents before rolling it out to the team?
options: Testing is only needed for compliance record-keeping
It reduces the number of placeholders required
It catches cases where a guardrail phrase gets ignored on messier or more ambiguous input
It automatically updates the version number
law-a1-reusable-prompt-frameworks-for-do.why: Testing across multiple real documents before rollout catches cases where a guardrail might not hold consistently on messier or more ambiguous input than the one it was designed against.

law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.q: Why does the protocol treat fabricated or misstated citations as their own explicit risk category, separate from general factual accuracy?
options: Citations take longer to check than other facts
Citations are the only thing AI tools get wrong
It simplifies the sign-off log format
It is the failure mode with the most severe real-world consequences on record and the easiest to miss, since a citation can look correctly formatted while referring to a case that doesn't exist
law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.why: Fabricated citations are named as their own category because they carry the most severe documented real-world consequences and can look completely correctly formatted while being entirely wrong.

law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.q: A junior associate verifies a citation against the primary source but doesn't record the check anywhere. What problem does this create?
options: There's no record the check ever happened if the work product is later questioned
None, as long as the check was actually performed
It only matters for citations used in oral argument
The AI tool will automatically log the check instead
law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.why: Performing a verification check but not logging it is a listed common mistake, since it leaves no record that protects the matter or the lawyer if the work product is later questioned.

law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.q: A citation is found to be "mostly accurate" but not fully confirmed against the primary source. How should the verification protocol treat it?
options: As passing, since "mostly accurate" is close enough for internal drafts
As blocking — it must be corrected or removed, not flagged and left in
As acceptable only if it will not be used externally
As passing if a second AI tool agrees with it
law-a2-verification-protocols-for-high-s.why: The protocol requires treating any citation, quote, or claim that fails full verification as blocking; it must be corrected or removed rather than left in with a mere flag.
